MR. HOWARD-SUGGESTED INCORRECT INFORMATION RESPECTING MOTION FOR PAPERS
speechtext:
I should like to raise a question of privilege touching some information which was given to the house yesterday in relation to my notice of motion for the production of papers No. 191 which related to correspondence between the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and any other person, group or organization, excepting any other department or agency of government.
In dealing with this motion the Associate Minister of National Defence said, as reported on page 11664 of Hansard:
I wish to inform the hon. member that there have been no correspondence, telegrams or other documents exchanged between the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation or any official thereof and any other person, group or organization relating to the application of the Canada Labour (Standards) Code or the deferment or suspension of any part thereof. Therefore I suggest to the hon. member that he might wish to withdraw his motion.
This I did. Subsequent to that, this morning, it came to my attention that there is certain correspondence, to which I should like to refer briefly. I have here a copy of a memorandum dated July 6, 1965, signed by one Guy Coderre. The address at the top of the memo is "Vice president, administration, Ottawa", of the C.B.C. and it is addressed to all the staff. The first paragraph reads as follows:
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
With the introduction of the Canada Labour (Standards) Code effective July 1st, 1965, it is
important that you be made aware of its implications on your conditions of employment with the C.B.C.
I have also a letter signed by one Clive B. McKee, director of industrial and talent relations of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, dated August 24, 1965 and addressed Mr. H. W. Sedgwick, Canadian vice president of I.A.T.S.E. While specific reference is not made in this letter to the Canada Labour (Standards) Code in those words, the second paragraph in the letter states that the corporation has applied to the Department of Labour for deferment of the act, and the implication is that that is the Canada Labour (Standards) Code.
I have another letter dated October 13, 1965 signed by Mr. C. T. Kelley, assistant director of industrial and talent relations of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, addressed to the same Mr. Sedgwick of I.A.T.S.E. In this letter specific reference is made to the code in the following words:
I am now able to confirm that, effective July 1, 1965, contract employees who work on a statutory holiday will be granted another day off in lieu, in accordance with section 31 of the Canada Labour (Standards) Code.
Finally, Mr. Speaker. I have a memorandum from the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation signed by Mr. D. J. van Bommel dated December 17, 1965 referring to a legal opinion they had received stating that certain people were not employees under the Canada Labour (Standards) Code, and under the circumstances were not covered by the code.
Based upon that, Mr. Speaker, my question of privilege is that there was erroneous information given to the house yesterday. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
That the question of the refusal to produce the documents referred to in notice of motion for production of papers No. 191 be referred to the standing committee on privileges and elections.

speechtext: In connection with the same matter, may I ask the Prime Minister whether he received any communication from Mr. Frank Maclnnis, president of the federation of farmers and businessmen of Inverness county. of the Dominion Coal Company for a fixed price or in accordance with whatever other arrangements might be made, could not be extended so as to take over DOSCO itself, since the Hawker-Siddeley group paid such a small price for the complex in the beginning. I understand it is also within the powers of the governor in council on appeal to ask to have a rehearing or a review. Therefore the very laudable object the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona had in mind is met by the law as it exists. Perhaps I should have known that, but the

fact is I did not. Apparently that deals with the first point.
The main discussion we had on clause 17 related to the question of whether there should be a larger quorum for the new kind of review, which is and will be of a somewhat more formal character than is provided in clause 17 subclause 4, because this is a new kind of subject matter which would come before this commission. [DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
The hon. member for Springfield suggested that there should be a larger quorum for these hearings than would be required for the hearings of one of the committees, and the hon. member for York South raised a question which I confess quite frankly-I do not apologize for this, I just confess it-I did not understand because I am not a lawyer. However, I think I have now been sufficiently instructed to understand it. The hon. member for York South seemed to imply that because it was provided in this case that a review could not be conducted by the committee which had heard the case originally no member of that committee could sit on the review. I have had the best legal advice I could obtain on the subject and was informed that all that the provision means in law is that the particular committee could not conduct the review but that any members of the committee, even those who were at the original hearing, are not prohibited from participating in the review. They would do so not as members of the committee but as members of the commission. I was also told that it had been a long-standing practice of the Board of Transport Commissioners in its hearings and reviews and it has frequently happened that some of those who have participated in an original hearing have also participated in a review.
The hon. member for Acadia raised a point, which was also raised by the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona and the hon. member for Peace River, that it might be difficult to constitute an appropriate review without having some of the members of the original committee participate in the review because they would have some expertise or at any rate greater knowledge of the particular mode of transport about which the review was to be conducted. I had thought that it would not be appropriate for those persons who had heard the case in the first instance to take part in such a review. I was told that there is a

distinction in law between a review and an appeal, that these reviews are not appeals and that there is not only no reason why someone who took part in the original hearing should not sit in review but that in many cases it is highly desirable that they should do so, and that this would be found to have been the practice of the board over the years. When one reflects on it I think it becomes quite apparent why this would seem to be appropriate.
I believe that this disposes of all the points except the one raised by the hon. member for Springfield. I would agree at once that in the case of a review under clause 17 subclause (4) it would certainly be necessary to have a larger number of commissioners sitting than would have sat on the original hearing. This would almost be essential, particularly as it would be desirable to have taking part in the review members of some of the other committees and particularly of the one related to the other mode of transport which was asking for the review. Therefore the only question that seems to be left of those that were raised is whether parliament should prescribe a higher quorum for such reviews than is done for the Board of Transport Commissioners at the present time.
I am told that on balance, in such reviews as have been conducted by the Board of Transport Commissioners over the years, it has always been the case that a large number of commissioners have sat than at the original hearing. In the new legislation and in the law as it now stands it is provided that the commission will have authority to set a larger quorum for any particular purpose if it wishes to do so and also that the Governor in Council can prescribe such larger quorum if he feels that the commission has not made adequate provision for such a review.
I find that this point was very carefully considered by the legal advisers of the Board of Transport Commissioners, of the Air Transport Board and the law officers of the Department of Justice, and that after they had weighed the pros and cons it was their view that the provisions in this regard, which had all been very carefully thought out, were adequate to meet all these needs. It was felt that an attempt to prescribe, in some particular circumstance, another quorum was not really necessary and that in view of the law and the practice in jurisprudence there would be no real doubt as to what would happen in fact.

Mr. Chairman, at this stage of the bill I shall suggest an amendment, the effect of which will be to introduce a new clause 20 and the subsequent clauses will require to be renumbered. I hope that my explanation for this action will commend the amendment to hon. members and will receive their support.
The bill before the house defines a national transportation policy. Inherent in that policy and essential to its success is the application of the principle that each mode of transport is to compete in order that there be an economic, adequate and efficient transportation system making the best use of all available transport modes in the country.
Many representations have been made about Bill No. C-231 and I think that the standing committee on transport and communications has done an excellent job. The committee certainly heard many submissions and it has approved many amendments in order to make the bill a more effective piece of legislation. But there is one very important development in the field of transportation which I personally should like to see the bill cover more fully, and I refer to the power of one form of transport to enter another transportation field and, as it were, to buy up and control the competition.
One of the more important principles in Bill No. C-231 is that whenever competition exists in transportation that competition should work to the advantage of the people of Canada. The interplay of competition certainly produces new and better ways of moving freight. It suggests new ways of reducing costs and is a strong restraining force on freight rates. We are dealing with a bill which will establish a new pattern of growth and development for all modes of transport under federal jurisdiction, and it seems to me that to fail to include in that bill a provision which will give some safeguard to the continuance of competition would undermine the bill's objective of competition in the transportation field
I acknowledge that there are situations in which common ownership of competing modes of transport may be in the public interest. For example, 1 can see certain situations in which the use of trucks by railways, not just in urban areas for pick-up and delivery but on
Transportation
intercity routes, may definitely establish a desirable integration of services. However, I also believe that we should empower the new Canadian Transport Commission to take a look at the ability of one mode of transport to gain control of a competing mode. I believe that the commission should have the authority in the public interest to restrain any policy or action by one mode of transport which would permit it to use its economic power to gain monopolistic control and to manipulate, as it were, competitive transport media.
In the Atlantic provinces and in western Canada the issue of control of one mode of transport by another is probably of greater public import than in central Canada. The extensive network of inland waterways and transportation services such as there is in central Canada does not exist in the Atlantic provinces or in the west. In the Atlantic provinces and in the west there are not as many trucking firms to compete with the railways.
I do not think that the entry of one form of transport into another can be dealt with by attempting to turn back the clock. I would be against disrupting the present pattern of services by suggesting that any form of transport be forced to divest itself of control of facilities which to date were legitimately acquired. I think we should perhaps accept the status quo as we find it at this time, but I also believe we have to look into the future and plan for the future. In particular, we should ensure that no sudden move can be made outside the authority of the Canadian Transport Commission to change radically the composition of the Canadian transportation industry by one mode deciding on its own how much of a competing mode it will acquire. I think that one form of transport should perhaps be able to experiment and to develop services in another mode, but I do not think that the public interest of this country will be served if moves are permitted in the transportation field which will seriously affect the amount of competition between the modes.
Accordingly, with that in mind I move:
That Bill C-231 be amended

Mr. Chairman, a couple of questions come to mind in this connection. Having had no advance notice, we have not had time to study this amendment. The first
January 12, 1967

question which comes to my mind, speaking as an individual, is this. Is the intent altogether good? This amendment brings up the whole subject of bigness of corporations and how we control it. It seems to me that often we concern ourselves with bigness and try to prevent it simply because we do not control it adequately through some public agency. In many instances I can see that more efficient production, if you like, in the transport field might be brought about by major companies controlling more than one mode of transport. We could accept bigness if there were adequate public control. That is one aspect of this matter that comes to mind.
I know it is late in the day to raise it but there is also the point that the two major railway companies already own many trucking firms. In my province, and I am thinking of the area between the Okanagan valley and the Pacific coast, the major trucking lines moving fruit in that area at the present time are owned by the railway companies. Have the minister and the hon. member for Port Arthur done any research into the point I have raised? What percentage of the major - trucking firms in the country is owned by railway companies? I wish to pose those two points to the minister.

May I immediately say a word in this regard. I think there are those in the trucking industry who would suggest that we should go much farther than this amendment goes and order the railway companies to divest themselves of all their trucking operations except those-representations of this kind have been made to me by some truckers-strictly ancillary to railway operations, such as delivery trucks in a town. I do not feel that in a bill like this we would want to embark upon such a fundamental change of practice as that would involve. I do not feel I should be willing to accept an amendment that would forbid future acquisitions. There is something in what the hon. gentleman says. Sometimes it may be more efficient to have one mode of transport owned by another. The public may be able to get better service that way.
What this amendment does, and I think very effectively, is to say that whenever anyone wants a hearing, when there is notice of acquisition of one mode of transport by another, a hearing shall be held to determine whether that acquisition is in the public interest and whether that amalgamation should take place. If the commission reaches the conclusion that on balance it would be in the

public interest to have that common ownership, it would be agreeable to the amalgamation. If the commission felt that amalgamation would create a monopoly apt to be injurious, it would not be agreeable to it.

industry, because since I was first elected to the house, that is on February 10, 1964, I have shown here on several occasions my interest for that industry.
As early as May 27, 1964, I put on the Votes and Proceedings of the house a notice of motion which appeared at page 25 of the order paper on June 3, 1964 and read as follows:
That, In the opinion of this house, the government should not implement the recommendations of the royal commission on transportation, better known as the MacPherson commission, which suggests, among other things, that the railway companies be free to set up a trucking system.

That motion did not come up for discussion, because the time allocated to the house for consideration of notices of motion was exhausted before it could be called by the Speaker.
On April 26, 1966, I asked the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) a question about the depreciation rate on trucks. On May 10, 1966, on the adjournment motion, I made brief representations to the Minister of Finance, asking him to reconsider maintaining the depreciation rate on trucks at 30 per cent instead of 20 per cent, as proposed in his budget speech. I can say that this intervention was successful, because the Minister of Finance revised his position on the depreciation rate on trucks and kept it at 30 per cent.
The amendment proposed by the honourable member for Port Arthur (Mr. Andras) reads as follows:
That Bill No. C-231, entitled an act to define and implement a national transportation policy for Canada, to amend the Railway Act and other acts in consequence thereof and to enact other consequential provisions be amended
(a) by inserting immediately after clause 19 on page 12 of the bill, as reprinted, the following: Notice of proposed Acquisition.
"20, (1) A railway company, commodity pipeline company, company engaged in water transportation, or person operating a motor vehicle undertaking or an air carrier, to which the legislative jurisdiction of parliament of Canada extends, that proposes to acquire, directly or indirectly, an interest, by purchase, lease, merger, consolidation or otherwise, in the business or undertaking of any person whose principal business is transportation, whether or not such business or undertaking is subject to the jurisdiction of parliament, shall give notice of the proposed acquisition to the commission.
I am glad to support this amendment for, to my mind, the trucking industry is of the highest importance to the economy of the country as a whole. It represents investments of over a billion dollars and, at the present time, in the province of Quebec alone, 55,000 employees depend on it for their livelihood.
Transportation
One Canadian out of 20 works for the trucking industry. One dollar out of 13, whether in wages, in salaries or in other revenues in the field of Canadian labour, comes from transport.
It is strange to note that former federal governments, since the advent of trucking, failed to take that industry into consideration in the various laws affecting the trucking interests in the field of competition.
However, a Liberal government has finally decided to review the whole national policy on transportation, taking into account all modes of transport including the trucking industry. They should be commended for creating such a precedent and I am convinced that the trucking industry will know how to show its appreciation for this significant and important step.
The various trucking associations in the country had been requesting a new national policy on transportation for a long time. As reported in the Canadian Trucking Association Review, dated April 23, 1965, the association will ask the federal government to introduce a new federal legislation authorizing provincial control boards, controlling extra-provincial trucking, to work together as a single unit. Such a legislation would therefore maintain provincial control boards as control agencies authorized to meet legally as a joint control board to deal with requests for extra-provincial trucking.
The July 14, 1965 issue of this association's review refers to the fact that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) is carrying on his series of speeches advocating the establishment of a national transportation authority, and it says that his appeal for such authority is the first logical statement of a truly positive federal approach to national transportation problems in many years.
It seems to me it is urgent to establish a national transportation policy in Canada. Even though the province of Quebec has set the example by passing adequate legislation, the fact remains that truck transportation has developed into a coast-to-coast operation and that all that legislation must be coordinated by a federal act.
The C.T.A., or Canadian Trucking Association, is satisfied with the bill under study and the amendment under discussion, since it made representations in that direction, that is for the following reasons:
First, to put an end to the multiplicity of hearings by many provincial boards.

Second, to remove the conflicts from one province to another because of the permits granted for the same extra-provincial company.
Third, to set forth regulations governing extra-provincial rates throughout Canada.
Fourth, to establish adequate legal control over the property transfers of extraprovincial companies.
Fifth, to put an end to the continued failure to apply the extra-provincial regulations, under the Motor Vehicle Transport Act.
In the province of Quebec particularly, the Transport Control Board supervises and controls a large number of owners of freight and passenger public transport companies.
Since the organization has already been set up, it is contemplated in the amendment to use the good offices of the boards now in existence in all provinces, for they have the experience and the qualifications to settle the problems of the trucking industry. They are the best existing organizations, and they are ready to co-operate with the federal government in the application of this transport legislation.
I am happy to point out that within Canada, Quebec now has, according to numerous public statements, the best legislation to protect the interests of both truckers and shippers. With only 11 per cent of the railroads in Canada, and with 30 per cent of the Canadian population, Quebec had to rely more heavily on highway transport. This explains the extraordinary development of this industry in that province.
The truckers associations have energetically and frequently protested against government paternalism in the shape of subsidies given to the railways. They maintain that the government should rather give subsidies to the shippers, who could then choose their own method of transport. The proposed amendment also aims to prevent intervention by the railways in the trucking industry. In a country where we extol freedom of speech, religion, movement, enterprise, the individual, private property, the press and freedom of choice with regard to political parties, we should also advocate free enterprise with regard to trucking companies and allow the various enterprises to compete freely.
Any user should be free to choose freely the method of transport he prefers. It is important that the income and expenditures of each method of transport should balance, each method of transport assuming the responsibility of its financial equilibrium. The
[Mr. Leblanc (Laurier) .1
words "freedom of choice of the user" are calling, of course, for competition, the only factor able to guarantee the user the lowest transportation rate, the conditions of a healthy competition and the financial balance of all the businesses.
That definition of free enterprise with regard to the trucking industry is supported by the "Union internationale des transports routiers" of Geneva, in its brief published in July 1962. As reported on page 13 of that document, it states:
On the other hand, the I.R.U. maintains as absolute prerequisites the two propositions hereunder which are liable to be accepted in all the economic systems, whether they are competitive or not. Prerequisite No. 1-Freedom of choice of the user.
The user must be able, in all freedom and taking into account the utilization factor which he defines for his own needs, to choose his method of transport and his transportation firm, or to decide that he will attend to the transportation himself.
Prerequisite No. 2-Financial balance.
The income and expenditures of each method of transport and each transportation firm must balance, each firm assuming the responsibility of its financial balance.
As a matter of fact, the role of the state is not to supplement private enterprise but rather to co-operate with it so as to improve the economy of the whole country. On April 20, 1966, when I commented on the budget, I made a statement of principle concerning the success of free enterprise in Canada and the need for continuation of this system in the country by adapting it to modem needs.
Here, in this country, we have the following statement made by the Newfoundland royal commission:
The C.N.R. and C.N. Transportation Limited should not be allowed to buy private trucking firms and they should not be permitted to have direct control over private trucking companies.
And, further on:
Their operations should be limited to freight transportation from one station to another and they should not be allowed to compete directly with private trucking.
Moreover, the brief submitted by the government of the province of Quebec to the royal commission on transportation in Canada, in December 1960, contains the following statement:
Section 302.
We believe that the railways should increase the efficiency of their service, trucking being for them simply a limited extension of their rail operations. But we object to the railways having control or a near monopoly of the trucking industry at the expense of the independent truckers and to the

detriment of the general public interest. As far as the province of Quebec is concerned, we already use for that purpose the provisions of the Transport Board Act (13 George VI, chapter 21, as amended, the General Regulations and amendments thereto). Section 303.
We remind the railways that their main responsibility to the Canadian people, historically, economically and socially, is to organize an efficient and economical system of railway transportation, and not to engage in the trucking industry. Consequently, we do not want them to touch the trucking industry in the province, except in certain exceptional cases, when required to fulfil efficiently their functions as railways.
Section 304.
We note the assurances given by the railways that their involvement in the trucking industry is not intended to drive out the independent truckers but rather to ensure an extension that would enable them to supply the Canadian public with a better, more adaptable and economical transport service than in the past.
Section 305.
Trucking, as a restricted complement to railway operations must not go beyond pick-up and delivery by railway-owned trucks in metropolitan centers and the principal cities.
In the United States, the railways are barred from trucking and the Financial Times of June 24, 1963 mentions, among other things: [English]
The Interstate Commerce Commission has told the C.N.R. competition, U.S. or Canadian, that no matter how short the route, it will not permit the railway to take over a truck line operating in the United States... all motor carriers in this country should be protected against rail controlled trucks. In great Britain, the 1962 Transportation Act also bars railway companies from entering the trucking field. Other countries have taken the same position: Germany, Holland, Italy, France and Mexico, among others. These countries have brought down legislation in this regard, leaving the shipping public free to choose their own method of transportation by land, thus providing true competition in the public interest. For the good of the country, it is essential that Canada should have a completely independent system of transportation by land, not only for the reasons which I have just advocated but also for labour considerations. Just imagine, Mr. Chairman, that all means of transportation in Canada-the railways, the bus and truck companies-would be controlled by the same interests, and a strike would occur. It would be a national disaster.
In concluding my comments, Mr. Chairman, I would like to call the attention of the house to the brief submitted in November, 1966, by the Canadian Trucking Association,
Transportation
Inc., to the standing committee on transport and communications with respect to Bill No. C-231. On page 14, paragraph 41, the brief mentions, among other things, under the heading "Access of railways to the trucking field", and I quote:
The independence and the competitive character oi the trucking industry are gradually disappearing. The purchase of trucking companies by the railways and the increasing importance of their trucking operations surely raises the question of future governmental policy in transportation legislation such as Bill No. C-231.
The following lines are found in paragraph 42:
This intrusion of the railways has been going on since 1946, with fluctuations by the C.P.R. between 1946 and 1948, and also in 1957-1958; in the case of the C.N.R. this dates back mostly to 1959.

The national transportation policy for Canada outlined in Bill No. C-231 inexorably brings the committee to study the extent to which the railways have entered the competitive trucking field and their position with respect to achieving control of the industry. We respectfully submit it is time that parliament-in view of the importance of the intrusion by the railways and the vast number of services controlled by the railway companies on the highways-went beyond high-sounding explanations concerning "co-ordinated trucking" or "integration of services".

The railway companies can achieve control in a given sector of the trucking industry simply by purchasing any one of six independent trucking companies, say, operating on a given line-

(7)	Every person competent to give evidence touching any matter under discussion in the committee shall be a compellable witness.
(8)	A person who gives evidence before the committee shall not without just cause (proof whereof shall lie upon him) refuse
(a)	to be sworn or make a statement;
(b)	to answer a question put to him by the committee or member thereof; or
(c)	to produce any document which he is required by the committee to produce.
I brought this matter to the attention of the committee before because in my opinion there is far too much apathy and indifference on the part of the government, members of this house, parliament, the press and the public regarding the extent to which parliament from time to time gives various commissions, boards and crown corporations almost uncontrolled power to regulate and deal with various aspects of our social and economic life. History shows that one of the saddest things about the loss of liberties is the fact that people who had the right and opportunity to do something failed to do so. Step by step, stage by stage and area by area we find that various rights which at one time fell within the control of the elected legislative body of this country have been filched away, eroded and whittled down.
As a result of the immense growth of governmental activity, obviously one can ask whether expert public servants are becoming the masters of the people they are employed to serve. Several other questions arise at the same time. Are not many administrators vested with authority to act as legislator and judge? Is this not a violation of the principles of separation of powers and natural justice? Perhaps the main question is that which involves the fundamental principle of democracy. Does not the growing pattern of administrative regulation undermine the ideal of

January 12, 1967
Transportation
representative government expressed through a popularly elected legislature?
As I said before, I recognize that in the kind of society and world in which we live it would be impossible for governments to operate without boards and tribunals vested with a certain amount of authority including the authority to make regulations and provide punishment for infractions of them. It would be utterly impossible for this or any parliament to deal completely with all the problems which arise and necessitate our attention. However, when we find that someone says, as often happens in companies or groups, I have been directed by this board or association to make a certain return, file certain documents and give some statistical information, we must conclude that this is not good when these directions are made under terms of regulations and enactments which are not part of the statutes. It is fantastic how often we as individuals are now told by appointed officials what we can or cannot do. This is not good because these people do not have a supernatural ability. There has been no laying on of hands. This happens because we as a legislative body have given this right to these people, and it is our responsibility in doing so to ascertain to what extent we can hedge this authority by safeguards in a way which will not interfere with the effective operation and function of these boards. We must make certain that the impact and result of the exercise of these functions do not harm those people who have sent us here.
Perhaps it is a good thing to have this conflict between elected representatives and civil servants. As a matter of fact I think there is far more conflict, as I think there should be, between us who sit in this chamber and those who are appointed. Only in that way can we have good government. However, the weapons and the conditions must be equal. This has been my complaint with regard to so many of the duties which we as members are asked to exercise by those we represent. We simply have not got the equipment, the knowledge and the assistance to do it. I am moving this amendment in that sense.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
As I said before, if the rules had permitted me to do so I would have included a clause by which expert assistance would have been made available to the statutory committee which I proposed. However, because this involved the expenditure of funds and private members are prohibited from so proposing I have not done so, but I would hope that if any

such committee is to be established the government would consider the provision of expert assistance. In a matter as complicated as this, where there are so few people who have adequate and expert knowledge, to set up a committee to do the things which I envisage as the work of this committee would be a completely fruitless exercise unless expert and knowledgeable people who would be in full and constant touch with the members of this committee were available.
I conclude by suggesting that this matter is one of which the government is well aware. When this house was dealing some time ago with the new proposed rules, which are now the interim rules under which the house is operating, I asked the Prime Minister about the possibility of setting up a committee on delegated authority. The answer which the right hon. gentleman gave me at that time indicated that he was well aware of the problem. He referred to Lord Hewart's book, "The New Despotism". He said he understood well the difficulty which faced the government. At that time he indicated that something might be done about the problem, but nothing has been done. I think the government realizes that the problem exists, but naturally the initiative must come from someone outside the government.
For this reason I propose in my amendment the establishment of a statutory committee, which is a novel concept in this country. This committee will sit from parliament to parliament thereby, I hope, building up for the duration of a parliament a body of men who will acquire an expertise and knowledge of this very complicated subject matter which will permit them not to sit as a court of appeal-of course this is absolutely unthinkable vis-a-vis the transport commission-not to obstruct the transport commission, but simply as a window through which we can peer at the operations of this commission. In this way we would be able to see to what extent their acts were having an impact on the social and economic lives of the people of Canada and to see what could be done if, in the opinion of this committee, things were happening which were not contemplated.
I am sure the minister will be the last one to disagree with me when I suggest that there are aspects and features in this bill of which he is not too sure. Where we will be three, four or five years from now is a question which I do not think he or anyone else in this country can answer. The future problems
January 12, 1967



which may face us in transportation can hardly be envisaged at this time in view of the departures which this bill is making. For this reason I urge the government, the minister and all hon. members, irrespective of their political views, to give what support they can to this proposal which I am moving in the form of an amendment.

Mr. Chairman, I wonder whether I could say a word or two? I have indicated that I am in great sympathy with the general objectives that the hon. gentleman has in mind and that were expressed also by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle. I think it would be desirable to have such a committee although I am not sure that I see why the standing committee on transport and communications of this house is not just as good as some other committee which might be created.
I am in sympathy with the idea which the hon. gentleman quite rightly put forward
Transportation
when he said that he could not include in the amendment the provision of expert assistance because it would involve the expenditure of money. I think I demonstrated my sympathy in this respect by facilitating the work of the standing committee when this bill was before it and by encouraging the commissioners of internal economy who paid for the expert assistance. It may turn out that it is my department which is paying for the expert assistance which the committee received and which was very good. I quite agree with those objectives.
I must say that I share fully the misgivings of the hon. member for York South about secret testimony. Because I am a Privy Councillor and he is not I have another misgiving about how secret the testimony would really be. However, I have a more fundamental objection to the amendment and I think I should indicate it right away because I do not think it is fair to give hon. members the impression that I would be able to support this amendment. I would not be able to support it for the reason that I am a member of the House of Commons and therefore could not support a measure which would permit members of the other place and the Crown to tell us what our rules in this house would be. When in the seventeenth century King Charles I went down to the Commons House of the parliament of that day to direct their activities the Speaker made the famous statement that he had no eyes to see nor ears to hear, and all of us know the rest of the story. I think it is just as objectionable for us to put in a statute which requires the assent, and therefore the dissent if they wish to disagree, of the hon. gentlemen for whom I have great regard but who are not us. They are not part of this house and I do not think it is any of their business to tell us what our rules should be. I believe it would be a terrible mistake to admit, even in a good cause, that they had any right whatever to tell us how we should conduct our affairs.
I think the hon. gentleman said he wanted to keep these things under the scrutiny of the elected representatives of the people. That is right, and we are the elected representatives of the people. Those other hon. ladies and gentlemen at the other end of this building are not the elected representatives of the people, nor is the representative of the Crown. It just seems to me that, in principle, it would be an abdication of our historic rights to attempt to import into legislation which required the assent of the other place an amendment to the

January 12, 1967
Transportation
rules of this house. If we decided later, or if another house decided later, it was desirable to change that, then it could not be changed without the consent of these other bodies.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
The leader of the house has on the order paper a motion, either in his name or is it in the name of the Prime Minister, to set up a committee to look into the rules. I have every sympathy for, and I would give my undertaking to support in principle, the setting up of a committee. I do not see why the present committee on transport and communications could not be given this function if it were given the extra assistance which I would be happy to see it given. We do have some very complicated matters coming before us. This is one of the most complicated measures we have ever had during my time here. I think we should provide for having someone with expertise to assist during any review which from time to time we might make.
I do not want the hon. gentleman to think 1 am not sympathetic to his objectives. I think they are sound and good. However, I believe the manner in which he would like to accomplish them, by a statutory provision which deals with the rules of this elected body, would be an abdication to others of that one small corner at least of that independence which is the foundation of self-government. For that reason, sir, I thought I should not waste any time in indicating why I could not vote for this amendment. I agree also with the point made by the hon. member for York South about taking secret testimony. I do not think it would work and I doubt that it would be desirable even if it would.

speechtext:
I do not intend to deal with the secrecy issue. I think the hon. member for Peace River will be dealing with that. I wish the minister had not spoken before I had an opportunity to make a few remarks on this matter because I was going to deal with the reasons for his objection to this amendment. I was hoping to advance my arguments before he had committed himself. I am going to put my arguments before this committee as sincerely and as frankly as I can.
The amendment moved by the hon. member for Peace River, which concerns the freedom of the people to run their own business, probably ranks in man's fight for freedom with all the other great steps that have been taken in the past. I include Magna Carta and all the rest. I will give my reasons for that statement, Mr. Chairman. If anyone tries to study seriously how a modern government can reconcile
[Mr. Pickersgill.l
itself to the modern type of economic system we have in the western world, he will find that the question boils down to how much control we can give to the people through their elected representatives. The answer given by the minister just now repudiates all the good work that he has done in the last two and a half years. In the last 48 hours I have made the statement to my colleagues and to people in the press gallery that in my judgment, with only ten years' experience in the house and a quarter of a century in the public life of this country, I have never seen a minister learn a complicated bill so quickly, express his ideas on it so clearly and be so flexible to the wishes of the committee, as the present minister.
We have had a demonstration here of virtuosity in mastering a complicated bill affecting the economic and social future of our country, while giving to the elected representatives in the committee and in the house a chance to work together in drafting a bill that is moving into a field about which very few of us know very much. This bill moves into the dark areas of the future. No one in this house could have surpassed the minister's penetrating mind in mastering this bill. I speak with personal knowledge because I worked on this matter for two years when I was a minister. I have not followed it as closely since, but I have had a long-time interest in the economics of transportation, particularly as they relate to railways. The compliment I have paid the minister, therefore, is one I think is owing to him without any qualification or modification.
However, I wish he had not made that last statement. I hope that we can maintain the attitude that has prevailed a while longer. If one studies the problems facing the governments of West Germany, Sweden, the United Kingdom and the United States, one will find that the problem of trying to make a parliamentary system work which grew out of the social and economic systems of the last seven centuries is not very easy. We in Canada are going through this same type of adjustment. If we tie ourselves down to the precedent of Charles I, then there is no solution to our problem. This is what the minister has done. If the men of our generation cannot recognize that adjustments have to be made in the traditional forms of democratic government to deal with the modern type of corporate structure, then our efforts in this house and in every other democratic government are a failure. This is the issue which the
January 12, 1967

hon. member for Peace River put on the record today in a speech which ranks, in its logic, with the best I have read over the last several hundred years of western history. Hon. members should re-read that speech.
We have in this house over the last two and a half years agreed, I suspect amongst all parties, to turn over tremendous powers of this parliament to a small group who have not in the past had a good record of protecting the interests of the people. We have agreed to turn over these tremendous powers because we do not see any other way of making the whole transportation system work efficiently. As the committee could gather from some of the speeches I made on the rationalization aspect of the bill, we want to even increase the powers we are turning over to this board.
Let us examine all the other crown corporations, the other agencies and boards which this parliament in its wisdom over the years has set up to carry out parliament's business. Let us look at the whole question of the delegation of powers by parliament. We will find one salient weakness and that salient weakness is, how do we touch base with them. We do not want parliament to interfere with their daily functions of administration. As the hon. member for Peace River made quite clear, we do not want to act as a grandstand quarterback in connection with the judicial part of their functions. However, if we are going to continue with the modern capitalistic system of the western world and democratic institutions, then we in this house have to examine our institutional procedures frankly.
To put forward the argument that just because this bill has to be passed in this chamber, has to be passed in the other place and signed by the Governor General, this takes away our power over our rules, can only be described by one word-farcical. All we ask in this amendment is that we let the people know that we have delegated these tremendous powers to a super board but that we are also preserving the right periodically to keep pace with them and to know what they are doing.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
We have accepted the fact that individually as laymen we are not competent to handle this question and have to have expert advice. From the past record we know what to expect in this parliament. Sometimes committees do not swing into operation for weeks or months after the commencement of the parliamentary session. Here is a perfect opportunity to show whether a democratic group can meet the
Transportation
challenge of our day and in a responsible, restrained way make some adjustment in our system to keep it moving a little faster and to keep it a little closer to the realities of today.
I do not think any member of this house who believes in the parliamentary system wants to see its power reduced by one iota. The proposal that we are making will preserve something of the power of the people through its elected representatives. This petty, picayune argument that because the Senators have to pass on our bill we lose our right to control our rules does not make sense to me.
We are trying to do something in this amendment with which the minister said he agreed and with which I am sure the government house leader agrees. I have also read remarks by the Prime Minister in which in effect he said he agreed with institutional changes. I believe that men of experience and good will want to see this institution remain sovereign but at the same time they want to make sure that the economic system of the country operates properly. We have to face the fact that our economic system is so complicated that we in parliament cannot deal with it efficiently. We must therefore agree to turn over this power to a super board and even give it more power. However, we do want the chance to preserve the sovereign right of parliament to control on behalf of the people their own affairs.
The setting up of a small committee to provide expert help would provide, as the hon. member for Peace River suggested, a window. But surely it would not be frosted over, because the 12 members of that committee representative of all parties would have some responsibility to the house. For example, if they thought something was wrong they would be able to come back here and take proper steps to right it, or if they wanted to make a proposal they could take the proper action. This would mean that the 17 members of this super board would know they were being watched by a group of people with competent advisers to see that everything possible was being done to bring about harmony with the guidelines we are trying to set down in this bill. We have the machinery through this committee, which will be responsible under the statute, to watch the operations of this board.
I suggest, and I hope the minister will reconsider, that in making adjustments to modern conditions Canada must not fall behind. We have seen what the French have done with their council of state in controlling the

January 12, 1967
Transportation
great bureaucracy of that country. We have seen what the Swedes and New Zealanders have done through their ombudsmen. These are small efforts to try to bring about some connection between the right of the individual to justice and protection against the bureaucracy that runs his country.
We are putting one complete sector of the economy of this country into the hands of a super board. Therefore in this day and age we must begin to think about institutional changes and of ways of maintaining and preserving in this house some sort of control over the board without interfering with its efficiency.
Therefore I hold to my statement that the argument presented that the amendment will bring forth the ghost of Charles I to haunt us in 1967 is nothing more nor less than specious.
I realize that the minister came to the house from the civil service, that the civil servants who run the country are able, sincere, usually dedicated and know so much more about each facet of government than do we as laymen, and that we have to have these people. But surely this group accepts the principle that a little bit of power must be left in the hands of the representatives of the people, and this is all we are asking for.
I realize that the statement of the minister was a reflection of his background, his long years in the civil service, but the fight that is going on all over the world today concerns whether men shall control the people they appoint. This question is being asked not only in western Germany, Switzerland, Sweden, the United Kingdom, France and the United States but also in Canada.
If we look at the situation in that great country in the Far East, China, what essentially are its people fighting about today? It is the same thing that we are debating this afternoon, Mr. Chairman. In China, which has a monstrous, huge civil service guiding the daily course of every factory and every farm, naturally there are going to be protests. There must be some way for the people to express their dissatisfaction. They even had to resort to the device of giving high school children free railway passes, free food and money to spend so they would watch factories and government offices and ask bureaucrats to explain why they did certain things. But what a crude technique to let the people express themselves and control their civil servants.
The great Prime Minister of China, Chou En-lai, tries to protect his bureaucrats because he knows they are essential to his country. On

the other hand, he sees the desire of the ordinary Joe to express his criticism of those civil servants from whom he takes orders in the schools, the universities, the streets, the factories and the farms. We cannot laugh at the red guards because we have used the same technique in the past. The Puritan movement in Great Britain in the 17th century was essentially the same sort of thing, it tried to change the character of man's nature by a social pressure that was open and forceful. This is never successful, of course, but nevertheless one sees the basic issue. If at times we in Canada think our civil service is slow and cumbersome, tied up with red tape, then I say go to China and see how bad it can be.
As I was saying, Mr. Chairman, we are not just debating the question of transportation. We are putting forward an amendment to try to improve the quality of democratic government in a day of great efficiency. If we cannot improve this institution in a practical way it is no good for people to go up and down the country pounding their chests and declaring that we have to reform parliament. The hon. member in his amendment is suggesting a reform of parliament. He also said that this same technique might work with the C.B.C. and with other crown corporations. No government likes to be told by the head of a crown corporation: Get out of our way; we have complete power to act.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
I do not hold it against anyone who sincerely believes that these crown corporations should not be criticized, because in many cases we have clearly delegated power to them under the act in question. As the hon. member for Peace River said, freedom is not usually lost in a revolution or war but through daily erosion. This erosion of power in connection with transportation will mean that a big chunk of our power will be delegated to a super board. We should maintain some sort of contact with the board. It would be a big help, not only to parliament but in improving the feeling across the country, if we could show that parliament is not myth-ridden, that it does not worship old fetishes. People think our attitude is that we do not let the Senate pass on anything that interferes with our rules.
Transportation by way of air, rail, pipe line, water, bus and truck affects the lifeblood of this nation. My request is made not as a Conservative member but as a member of this house who has consulted with his colleagues. I hope there is support from all sides of the house. We hope that the Liberals in the house
January 12, 1967

will agree with the principles we raise. We are trying to preserve the rights of parliament in some small measure. We accept the principle that efficiency must predominate, but the right of the individual to express himself in our system must be preserved.
This amendment may not be very good. We do not know whether it will work but it is the best we can do. Some of us have laboured over the transportation problem for a long time. We have other amendments to move but none of them is more important in principle than this one. I think the hon. member for Peace River, when he introduced this matter on December 20 and again today, has made his mark in the history of parliament. That mark will long endure. I pay my respects to him and I pay my respects to members in all parties who sat on the railway committee, who listened to a great deal of evidence and who showed such flexibility and willingness to produce a good bill. Many amendments were accepted in that comiittee.
I pay my regards to the staff. They must have worked extremely hard trying to find legal and statutory answers to the problems raised. There was an example where we all worked together. I hope the minister does not out of hand, as he sometimes does, produce an argument turning down the suggestion we are making. I think the hon. member for Peace River can meet the arguments of the hon. member for York North-

I beg your pardon, York South. I think the arguments can be met. Essentially we are trying to introduce into this house an institutional change, one that may set a precedent for other boards. The problem we have in this country is a problem faced all over the world. I do not want to quote authors and studies. Many articles and monographs by exceptionally able people who are worrying about this problem have been produced. In his last speech on this subject in this country, the high commissioner for Great Britain pleaded with the senior civil servants of this country to please give the elected representatives a little power. That plea came from a man who had held five portfolios in the United Kingdom and who had spent several years in Canada. I think he respected us. For him to make that type of plea to our civil servants shows that he feels our problems are the same as those of the United Kingdom.
The United States is worse off than we are and the French, of all, are the worst off. The problem must be met. I hope the minister will 23033-741
Transportation
not rush in too quickly to express his views. We have considered this matter with great humility. It does not affect our freedom in this house but I think it does show to the people of Canada that we are trying to preserve parliament's rights. In the interest of efficiency we are not trying to stop any board from having complete power. We are trying to be responsible and we are trying to be constructive.
I hope this amendment is given serious consideration by the minister. We want to express our views on it strongly. I will not deal with the matter I raised last night having to do with the minister's progress on the bill, because that matter is not as important as this amendment. I appeal to the minister to maintain the reputation he has established during the last two and a half years. He has a reputation for having mastered the principles of the bill. He explained it fully to us in committee. In his dealings with the bill he has been willing to adjust, and this adjustment has been met by all sides. As a result of the minister's attitude we have reduced to a minimum the heat that might be generated by many matters. Parochial and regional interests have been reduced to a minimum in trying to get a good bill. We know we are moving into a new field.
We hope that as the years go on this bill will prove to be a good one and that the board will obtain the necessary personnel, who must be hard to find. We hope that the board's decisions will set good precedents for future boards. To keep in touch with the people, to get viewpoints, we hope that a responsible pattern of communication will be organized. I hope that along the channels of communication positive ideas may flow. I will not press that matter at this time.
The essential point is: will parliament accept the challenge? Can we mend our ways and break even a little with tradition? Can we let the committee operate under a statute and give it permanent employees loyal not to the government but to the committee so that those employees can keep in touch with the workings of the commission? They ought to be competent to funnel ideas either way in language which makes sense to the layman. We hope that the 12 members on the committee will develop over a period of years the same sort of working spirit that we have developed in this committee so that it will be a matter of pride to be a member of that permanent committee of the house and so that men will fight to be the representatives of their party on the committee. If they develop

January 12, 1967
Transportation
that pride we shall not be juggling hon. members around to fill in slots.
I think this committee deserves to have members from all parties in the house and from all over Canada. I confess that the ideas in this resolution are borrowed partially from Australia, from where we get the statutory concept, and partially from the United States where there is a full-time staff. Even if the ideas are borrowed, these problems still exist in Canada. They exist not only in Canada but all over the world and it is our responsibility to do what we can toward solving them. This amendment is only a small step in meeting these problems, especially the problem of control of people exercising delegated authority. I think this amendment is a worth-while first step.

speechtext:
I should like to say a brief word. It would be most ungracious of me not to express appreciation for what I think is probably the greatest compliment paid to me since I have been in public life. It comes from the other side of the house but that does not make me less appreciative of it. The fact that it was paid by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle who, like me, is not ashamed to be partisan, makes it all the more touching.
Notwithstanding what the hon. member said and notwithstanding my genuine appreciation of his remarks, he has not altered the view I have expressed. I should not like the hon. gentleman to have the wrong impression. That is why I rose at once. I would not want him to think that I had made a hasty or snap judgment. After all, the hon. member for Peace River very considerately gave us a preview before Christmas of what he proposed to do. I have had, therefore, as we all have had, a good deal of time to reflect on the matter.
I thoroughly agree with the objective. I think that we should have a committee. We on this side of the house, since coming to office, have given evidence of our disposition. The Prime Minister and the Minister of National Defence instituted the kind of defence committee of this house that we have never had before. Under the new temporary rules we have had a considerable overhauling of the standing committees of the house.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
I think there has been more good work done by committees of this house in the last year or two than at any time in the nearly 30 years during which I have been observing parliament or sitting in it. The time is long

past when we should get expert and independent assistance in committee work when committees are dealing with complicated matters and the members themselves cannot be expected to have at their fingertips the necessary expertise. With all this I completely agree. What I cannot agree with is the view that we are so undisciplined in this house, which is elected by the people, that it is necessary to have people appointed in another place participating in making rules for us and that those rules should be embodied in a statute. Incidentally, if we really mean what we say when we declare that this house is an independent house and master of its own affairs, such a statute could not be enforced anyway. Who is the policeman who will come in here and enforce the statute on this independent assembly? This is why, when I talk about Charles I and the independence of parliament, I am not talking about some old fusty thing in the seventeenth century.
It is this aspect of the matter which I believe the mover of the amendment and the hon. gentleman have got wrong. I cannot see how these provisions would have any more sanctity if they were established by statute than if they were established by a standing order of this house alone. We discipline ourselves, though sometimes not as effectively as we should. But if our discipline in this house is not effective I do not think it would become more effective if we called in outsiders to discipline us, or purport to discipline us, or make rules for us as though we were children.
It may be that the composition of the present committee is too large. It may be that the composition of all the standing committees is too large for effective work to be done. If all committees were composed of a dozen members instead of 24 members we should not have to wait so long for quorums and it would be possible to concentrate more on getting the work done and on getting it done more expeditiously. With all this I agree. But I say, do not let us abandon the most fundamental of all the rights of the elected representatives of the people, that is, our own corporate independence in this house.
The hon. gentleman said I had been flexible and tried to meet suggestions from whatever quarter of the house they had come. I have done that just as much in this case and I intend to continue doing so. This does not mean that if I am unable to see eye to eye with hon. gentlemen opposite on all of their suggestions I have suddenly changed my character. It seems to me we have two principles here, both fundamental principles, but that in this amendment they are in conflict with each other. One is the principle that this house should scrutinize the administration. That is what we are primarily elected to do. With that part of the amendment I completely agree. I do not think we are doing it as effectively as we should and I agree with the hon. member for Qu'Appelle that we should do a better job in controlling, checking and auditing the administration of this country-and I do not use the word "auditing" in a narrow sense. After all, though I went there as a stranger I represent one province in this country which just before it became a province had no elected representatives at all for 13 years-the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo nods-during one of the saddest interludes in the history of free institutions in the British Commonwealth.
They had an efficient government. They had devoted public servants who carried out their jobs according to their lights. But there was no audit, no check on the part of the public. It was a bad system, a wrong system, and we are here to see that it never happens again in this country. But this is our job as the elected representatives of the people and we should do it ourselves by our own activities. We can amend our own rules and if they do not work we can change them again without praying some appointed people elsewhere to change them. Here we have a conflict with the good principle that it is our duty to audit, check and control the administration. But it is our duty to do this ourselves independently, and we do not need to have anyone outside this chamber to do this.

The hon. member says parliament. I have more confidence in the people's elected representatives than my hon. friend seems to have, since I do not think it is necessary for appointed individuals, not accountable to the public, to have something to say about what this house does or, for that matter, about what a particular commission as important as this one has to do.
If an effective surveillance of the work of this commission is required, I submit that the way to do it is not by appointing another special committee but by strengthening the over-all system of standing committees of this house so that we develop a proper system of specialist committees composed of members who have developed an expertise over the years in the subject matter of the committee, backed up by an appropriate professional and permanent staff.
The example of other countries has been brought forward-France, Germany, the United Kingdom, the United States. Their trend is not to set up, piling one on top of the other, further special and joint committees. Instead, what they have done is to create a permanent system of standing specialist committees. The appropriate committee is given the job of looking after all matters coming under the jurisdiction of the legislature pertaining to the subject matter in question, including the operation of their equivalents of this transportation commission.
There is no question that what this House of Commons needs to have at this time is a greater degree of what political scientists call legislative oversight. This is the great lack, the great gap in our present system. The elected representatives of the people clearly must have a greater degree of control and a greater ability to look into and supervise the operations of the bureaucracy which has so much to do with the way the government of this country is carried out. Again I submit that this cannot be done by having a series of
January 12, 1967

special committees and joint committees dealing with limited subject matters, the members of which have to divide their attention between them and standing committees.
We have already had some experience in the past year and a half under the provisional rule changes of how a surveillance of this type could be effectively carried out by permanent standing committees. The broadcasting committee has already had before it the Board of Broadcast Governors; it has already had before it the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. Yet it also covers a broad subject matter in the field of broadcasting and the arts. Surely it could continue to do this. Surely the transport committee of this house could do the same thing as it has already begun to do with respect to Canadian National Railways.
To give a further example, the finance committee has looked into the workings of the Expo Corporation. This again, I submit, is the appropriate way to carry out this objective, this aim with which I think we are all in agreement. The thing to do is change the rules of this house, not just to permit a special committee to look into the workings of this commission but to make sure that permanent committees are set up and in operation within a certain period after the opening of a new parliament, that they are given the right to have a permanent staff, not only by special resolution of this house with respect to a particular subject matter referred to it, that they are given the right to set up subcommittees so that a more careful examination may be made of special subjects. In fact, I see no reason why the transport committee of this house could not, under the rule changes I am suggesting, have a subcommittee to pay special attention to the workings of this transportation commission.
It seems to me to be contradictory to talk about giving greater authority to the elected representatives of the people to look after and oversee the workings of the federal bureaucracy, and at the same time make the coming into effect and the changing of the method of carrying out an examination by a special committee subject to the approval or disapproval of a group of people who are appointed to age 75 and are not accountable in any way to the people of this country. We have been talking about centennial presents for the people of Canada. I think one of the finest centennial presents we could give the Canadian people is a modern effective parliamentary system which is truly relevant to the needs of governing a modern technological state such as Canada is today. In any case I stress the fact that in my estimation it is not too important whether the committee is based on a statute or whether it derives its authority from the ordinary rules of the house. What is important is the body of precedent and practice built up over the years by committees

On reading the minutes of the proceedings of the committee on transport and communications at the time it was studying the bill now before this committee I found some comments which are very apropos. This is our concern, that if the commission is almost totally isolated from the views of the general public it is possible for them to become overgrown with the tangle of technical preconceptions to the point where they do not see the broader picture.

Mr. Chairman, I have an amendment I should like to suggest. I believe it would be numbered as new clause 39A, copy of which has been handed in at the table. Originally we intended to move it as an amendment to clause 20 and number it 20A. It was considered wiser, however, to bring it in at this stage of our consideration of the bill. The

amendment seeks to provide the commission with power to lay down the conditions under which abandonment can take place.
During previous sessions private members bills have been introduced to this effect. Invariably time did not permit a decision to be reached in respect of any of these attempts to establish this principle in our railway legislation. It is a principle which should be established, because where abandonment is carried out in an unplanned and unregulated manner some very unfortunate experiences occur in various parts of the country. I might state again the experience we had in my part of Ontario when the New York Central Railway abandoned their Courtright line which extended across the counties of Lambton, Middlesex and part of Essex. The business on the line had diminished until there was very little operation of the railway. The company was granted permission by the Board of Transport Commissioners to abandon this line.
For a number of years before abandonment took place the company had neglected to keep the fences and other equipment along the line in repair. When they were granted permission to abandon the line they tore out the rails, the ties, and any usable culverts. The fences were wrecked by the power machinery used to demolish the structures along the line. The line when abandoned was left in terrible shape. It became an eyesore and a nuisance to the whole area it crossed. Whether or not they have had farming experience, I am sure hon. members will realize that when a railway line crosses a rural area it separates the farms into two parts part being on one side of the railway line and part on the other side. So long as the railway line is in operation the Railway Act provides that the railway company at its own expense shall maintain the fences along the right of way and shall provide drainage from one part of the farm to the other; that is, the railway line is not permitted to impede drainage of any kind. Each farm must be provided with a properly maintained crossing across the railway line.
The Board of Transport Commissioners has ruled that once a line is abandoned they have no further jurisdiction over the right of way. In this case it reverts to the status of any other property held in the province or in the municipality. Any rights, privileges, and protection which persons along the railway previously had enjoyed under the Railway Act disappear. The farmers cannot cross these rights of way, fenced or unfenced, without
January 12, 1967

trespassing. The fences fall down; they are allowed to deteriorate; livestock can wander at will, and the right of way grows up in brush and weeds. No one can do anything about this, and that is the point I wish to stress here.
Questions have been raised concerning the competence of the parliament of Canada to deal with this matter, on the ground that once a right of way ceases to be used as a railway it then reverts to the status of private property, and comes under provincial jurisdiction. I submit there still remains a question concerning jurisdiction over these abandoned lines. I am not learned in the law and therefore I am not in a position to argue the case. I have found it quite difficult to arrive at what I thought was an equitable way of dealing with this matter. I have a suggestion to offer to the committee which I think would meet the situation. I think we all agree that there are in western Canada some of these unprotected lines. I am not saying all of them should be abandoned by any means, but everybody agrees that some of them should be abandoned and might well be abandoned as quickly as possible because all they are doing is costing the taxpayers of Canada money for a very, very inadequate return.

In one case it was suggested it would depend upon the number of bushels hauled; but when I asked whether this was a formula, I think the minister said that perhaps it would be a guide but that it was not a definite formula which could be used. by the new transport commission would like to know by what formula they must gauge their own position in order to know whether or not their line may be saved. Surely the minister is well aware of the fact that in recent years many of these branch lines have experienced a tremendous upswing in the movement of grain. Perhaps some of them would qualify now whereas a few years ago they may not have. The future looks bright in respect of huge grain shipments. In this regard it may be that some of these lines should be protected until 1975.
Another question which comes to mind with regard to rail line abandonments is the way in which the C.N.R. and C.P.R. do their cost analyses. They take the total cost of moving the grain from the end of the line which will be abandoned to the point at which the line reaches the main line. They call that the offline cost. Then they take the movement of grain from the point at which the branch line joins the main line, take it from there to the lakehead or to Vancouver, and call this the on-line cost. Then the total of the two is the total cost of moving the grain. They compute the figures in respect of revenue and come up with a loss figure. If one were to project the thinking of the railways in respect of costs alone, he could prove that every branch line in western Canada should be abandoned, if it could be shown that they were losing money on the Crowsnest pass rates.
When talking about branch lines one must consider the effect of the branch lines on the Crowsnest pass rates, because if all branch lines were abandoned the Crowsnest pass rates in effect would be destroyed. One thing I should like to make clear is that western Canada will not allow total abandonment of all branch lines. No matter how insignificant a branch line may be, the method which the railways use is a method by which they cannot prove that every branch line should be abandoned, unless somebody can get the exact figures from the railways or from the Board of Transport Commissioners in respect of the number of load-ton-miles the grain is hauled, and the exact cost of maintaining the track.
There are lines in my constituency which may be 60 miles in length and on which there may be only 24 trains a year. It is logical to assume that the cost to maintain that track is less than it would be to maintain track over which a train runs three times a day. But does the C.N.R. use an average figure in computing the cost of maintaining that track? No, they do not. These are things somebody should be
