Some time ago the former president of the C.N.R.'s Mr. Donald Gordon, made the "grain on the move" speech in Winnipeg. He said that 1,000 carloads of grain moved 60 or 70 miles on the railroad in one year could be moved more easily and at less cost by truck. This brings us into a very interesting situation. I did not accept that figure a few years ago and I still do not accept it. I am not computing the costs of the C.P.R. and the C.N.R., but if they maintain that a truck can move that amount of grain that distance for half what it costs the railroad to move it, then it looks as if they are operating their trains inefficiently. I have no objection to this, however, if they want to do it in this way. If the C.N.R. and C.P.R. want to abandon a line because they think they can haul the grain out at less cost by their own trucks, then let them do it. Then our Crowsnest pass rates will be maintained.

The point here is that if the railways say they can haul the grain at less cost by truck, then I have no objection if the line along which the farmers are farming is going to be abandoned, because this would maintain the Crowsnest pass rate for all farmers. If branch lines are abandoned, farmers will have to bear the cost of moving their grain an extra 60 or 70 miles at a cost of, to use the former president's figure, five cents to fifteen cents per bushel, depending on how large the farmer's truck is or how much he must pay to the commercial trucking firm he must hire.
Many roads in western Canada are capable of carrying trucks loaded with a thousand bushels of wheat, but these roads are few and far between in the outlying areas. Most of the good roads run adjacent to main lines of the railroad. The poor roads are located in those areas close to branch lines which are to be abandoned. As a result, the greatest burden created by a branch line abandonment would fall on those farmers producing grain in the outlying areas. In most cases the main lines of the railways in western Canada run through the best agricultural land. As a result the farmer producing the best and most grain is close to the main line, whereas the farmer who will bear the greatest cost is producing the lower grades in the outlying areas.

Let the trucking companies haul this grain, just as they are doing in one area in my constituency. The railway company has established a precedent in this regard. In one area the Wheat Board instructed the railway company to move the grain from certain licensed elevators. The railway company had not kept the track in repair for many years and said they did not want to run a train on that line because of its state of disrepair. It indicated that the cost of repairing one bridge would be in the neigbourhood of over $60,000. I do not suppose the company has driven one spike along that line since it was originally put in. The company did not want to spend that kind of money on this line, which was up for abandonment. In this particular case the grain had to be hauled by truck for some 50 miles and the C.N.R. paid the cost of that haulage. The cost was not paid by the grain company which purchased the wheat for the Wheat Board, nor by the farmer who grew the grain.
Surely the company has established a precedent that we should recognize. Any grain elevator which is necessary, whether it is located near a line that is up for abandonment or adjacent to a main line, should remain licensed as an agent of the Wheat Board to receive grain from the farmers. The railway companies should move that grain from those elevators by truck if they can do so more cheaply.
Surely when a railway company makes application for a branch line abandonment it should be obliged to prove that it can move grain more cheaply by truck than by rail. That is the test which should be applied in these cases. I am not suggesting this should apply to those areas located within 10 or 15 miles of a main line, because the farmers I am sure would gladly haul the grain that distance. But in those areas where farmers will have to move their grain 50 miles or more from an abandoned line to a terminal point, if the railway companies suggest they can move the grain more cheaply by truck, a fleet of trucks should be brought in to move that grain. The railway companies have been allowed to move into the trucking business. Surely this is the only way the Crowsnest pass rates can be maintained in western Canada.

Let us consider the movement of grain. Mr. Gordon dealt with this subject in a speech he delivered in Winnipeg. He referred to the modernization of grain handling and movement, and talked about speeding up this process in order to save money. If Mr. Gordon feels that the railways can save money by moving grain by truck, then we should permit the railways to do so whenever branch lines are abandoned.
This parliament should never pass an act so rigid it cannot be adjusted with changing times. Let us allow rail line abandonment on the prairies, provided the railway companies haul the grain at Crowsnest pass rates. If the railway companies say they can haul the grain more cheaply by truck, let us allow them to do so.
The railway companies have suggested they can move up to 1000 box cars of grain per year by truck for approximately 4 cents to 5 cents per ton mile cheaper, which represents a saving of about one third. I suggest in any rail line abandonment application the railway companies should be obliged to indicate how much can be saved by moving the grain by truck, and compare that to the inconvenience caused by total abandonment of a railway service. If the abandonment of a branch line creates an excessive hardship or social upheaval in a production area the commission should rule that the elevators concerned remain licensed agents of the Wheat Board, and that the grain be moved by truck. We must adjust to the times. We must make our legislation sufficiently flexible to allow these changes to take place, in order to speed up grain movement, resulting in greater efficiency of grain handling.

Mr. Chairman, I shall only take two or three minutes to deal with clause 42 of Bill No. C-231.
To my mind, the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Horner) has brought up important points, on which additional comments could be made.
The title of the clause is as follows:
Abandonment and rationalization of lines or operations-uneconomic branch lines.
Mr. Chairman, the whole clause is ambiguous if it is intended to set the standards, the criteria for establishing whether or not a line is to be abandoned. In my opinion, it boils down simply to profit or loss. I believe the whole matter is unfair to the Canadian public and that the agreements reached with the railroad companies, at the time they were granted what we know, was trickery of sorts. Basically the standards or criteria should be: does the economy of the region concerned still need railroad services? Whether or not the services are profitable becomes secondary, because we must go back to the basic principle.

Mr. Chairman, the railroad companies entered into a contract with Canada, as we know. They were granted the equivalent of gold mines, rights to untold natural resources. Then, with their profits in those fields, they launched out in other fields of endeavour such as maritime transport, hotels, air transport, mines and other related businesses.
Today, now that all the frosting has been eaten off the cake, operating profitable lines,
I believe it would be unfair for them to abandon the unprofitable lines. I feel this would not be respecting the agreement entered into in earlier days, giving railways the advantages we know, at the price we had to pay. We need only remember, for instance, how many governments were defeated because of these concessions made to the railway companies.
I do not know whether this idea can be added as an amendment, but I say to the hon. Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill), that the future commission should at least be given detailed instructions, to the effect that the criteria, the norms or the standards determining whether or not a particular line may be abandoned, must not necessarily stem from profitable or unprofitable operation. In my opinion, we should ask ourselves: does the economy of our country and the economy of this area depend upon railway service? Could another means of transportation serve that area as efficiently as the railway? If the answer is no, then railway service must be maintained-whether profitable or not-because it would be unreasonable for the country to have given the railways the advantages they have been granted-which have enabled them to pile up an extraordinary amount of money-and today, because certain lines are operating at a loss, to say to them: "Well, get out of there with your little gold mine and let the people living in that unprofitable area tighten their belts." Besides, some lines are profitable, and to be logical right to the end, if the unprofitable lines were abandoned, then the railway companies would have to disgorge and pay the government the profits made by operating the truly profitable lines.
I therefore submit to the hon. minister that a specific clause might be added, establishing that the economic interest of the country and the area concerned must receive first consideration or, at least, set out in one form or another, specific directives for the members of the commission, so that when they are called upon, their ruling will not be based solely upon cold statistics showing whether or not the line is profitable.

maintopic: "LABOUR GAZETTE"-DELAY IN DELIVERY OF FRENCH EDITION
"LABOUR GAZETTE"-DELAY IN DELIVERY OF FRENCH EDITION
speechtext:
Yesterday, Mr. Speaker, I posed a question to the Minister of Labour, for the seventh or eighth time in the last 12 months, asking why the

DEBATES	January 12. 1967
French edition of the Labour Gazette is always three or four months late. Up until two or three months ago the minister answered that things were supposed to be improving, and on one occasion he even mentioned that by September or October both issues would be published simultaneously. Yesterday the minister answered my request, after I had suggested that a special committee should be appointed to take care of this matter, by saying that he was opposed to appointing such a special committee. He said that we had an effective committee of the house and that we do not need another. Then he added that this matter has made good progress up to now, and the French edition has been delayed because the chief of the translations section was taken ill.
I am not satisfied with that answer. I hold the Minister of Labour in high regard; he has great responsibilities and I have much respect for him. But I must say I am disappointed, even shocked, with the answer he gave yesterday. His answer looks to me to be some kind of wishy-washy soporific excuse. He was trying to evade something, to camouflage something. I cannot go for that, Mr. Speaker. I think the minister should have said to me, "Somebody has forgotten to do what he was ordered to do". There is no reason for having the French edition coming out two or three months late. Two or three years ago both editions came out together. I understand that the section needs translators. Having made some inquiries, I can find half a dozen translators in 48 hours.
Somewhere I think there has been negligence. I do not blame the minister personally; probably he is badly informed by somebody. He should try to find solutions to the difficulty right away. Let me put it this way: I do not see why, in the next two months, both editions cannot come out together. If this question offers such a great problem, then I offer to solve the problem for the minister, and I will not charge anything. I will do it for nothing. I shall find translators to do a good job.
Mind you, I am not begging for special favours; I hope the minister understands that. This is something to which we are rightfully entitled. Also, many complaints from my province have come from labour organizations which feel they ought to have the French edition simultaneously with the English. They do not understand why we do not get the French edition.
January 12, 1967	COMMONS
There is another reason why I bring this matter up. Not having the edition simultaneously with English gives ammunition to the separatists. It puts in an awkward spot those of us trying to tell our people that confederation is not so bad after all, that there is a future in confederation, I bring this to the attention of the minister and I urge him to give the necessary orders to those in charge of the translations bureau, to see to it that we may have the French edition as soon as possible. When I say as soon as possible I think of the next month, or perhaps of the next two months, at the latest.
If what I ask is not done I must tell the minister that every month I shall be standing up and posing the same questions, and that I might lose my patience. I have tried always to be courteous to the minister, but I might be mean at times because I feel somewhat annoyed. I know the minister is used to all kinds of threats, but this, I think, has lasted long enough and it is high time it were settled. I might go to the parliamentary committee mentioned by the minister, if the minister cannot solve the problem, and bring this matter to their attention.
I beseech the minister, for goodness sake, to find a solution, so that we shall not have to hear what we have listened to in my province month after month. This matter really gives wicked ammunition to the separatists.

speechtext:
I listened to the hon. member for Trois-Rivieres with a great deal of interest. Despite his indignation I cannot visualize any situation in which his patience would be strained to the point at which he would become discourteous. I do not think that is a characteristic which he will ever display in the house.
I share his feeling, as one closely attuned to the problems of confederation, that the greatest defence we have against the spread of separatism in the province of Quebec is the intelligence and integrity of the labour movement. There are a number of young men and women joining organized labour in the province who will be exposed to the sensible arguments of the leading labour figures who endorse the idea of a united Canada, and the fact that the Labour Gazette is not made available all the time in both official languages of this country, simultaneously, can become a very serious bone of contention and 23033-743

I realize that the hon. member has brought up this question on several occasions. I think the time has come to cease making excuses. I think we must find a solution to the question of producing documents and periodicals as important as the Labour Gazette simultaneously in the two languages. I repeat that labour is of paramount importance at this moment, and I believe that all who belong to the organized labour movement in Quebec should have equal opportunity to read the Labour Gazette in the other of the official languages, just as it is available in the English language.

maintopic: GOLD MINING ASSISTANCE-QUEBEC-POSSIBLE SOLUTION OF PROBLEMS
GOLD MINING ASSISTANCE-QUEBEC-POSSIBLE SOLUTION OF PROBLEMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on January 11 that is, yesterday, I asked the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) whether he had been informed of the brief submitted to certain government members including the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Pepin), by the northwestern Quebec chambers of commerce with regard to the gold mining problem. The Val d'Or-Bourlamaque and Malartic city councils have endorsed that brief submitted in March 1966.
At the end of November last, the northwestern Quebec regional economic council and the muncipalities directly affected by the gold mining problem also submitted their own brief calling for increased assistance to gold mining.
Now I believe, Mr. Speaker that the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act expires in 1967. It must be not only renewed, but improved by increasing subsidies to the gold mines. We know that the price of gold has remained steady since 1935 at $35 an ounce, American funds, which is equivalent now to $37.75 an ounce. We also know that the cost of living index has increased from 1

January 12, 1967
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion to 240 since 1935. We know that the wages paid the miners working in the gold mines are 25 percent less than wages paid in other mines and 15 per cent less than those paid in other industries. It is important to know at the earliest moment what the government's intentions are concerning its gold mining policy.
The public bodies which last year presented briefs to the government on gold mining represent more than 110,000 people dependent in one way or another upon the mining activity in northwestern Quebec and the whole economy of the area feels the rise and fall of mining operations.
The Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act should provide for the maintenance and development of active mines and the opening of new mines, which would boost the economy of this area.
The chambers of commerce, the municipal councils and the regional council of northwestern Quebec ask nothing else but a better standard of living for miners and their families. In that connection, the brief says:
After considering the present situation, we came to the conclusion that a revision of the act passed in 1948 and amended a few times until 1958, when a 25 per cent increase in subsidies was granted, is imperative, and our request is not for the purpose of enabling this industry to pay greater dividends. It wants first of all to take into consideration that we must now face a shortage of competent labour in gold mines because of salaries which are not competitive with other fields of industry.
We can say, as proved by figures, that the money received under the Gold Mining Assistance Act, far from being used to pay dividends to shareholders, has been used to give a better deal to workers; furthermore, only salary increases given to workers represent more than 2.2 times the sums received under gold mining assistance.
We must consider that this year, the workers, like their fellow-workers in Ontario, will demand the 40-hour week, and our mines will have to grant the same treatment as given elsewhere; this burden alone, especially for marginal mines, could force them to close their doors; that is the economic reality.
Considering this new need, new obligations which must be assumed in a changing society, which requires more for public services, especially education, we consider that the time is favourable for adjustment of subsidies to gold mines so as to enable them first of all, and this is the main motive of our pressure, to give their employees the salary increases which will enable them to compare their case with what is done in other areas of industry.
The government should therefore inform us, as soon as possible, of the policy it intends to follow concerning gold mines.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jack Davis (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
maintopic: GOLD MINING ASSISTANCE-QUEBEC-POSSIBLE SOLUTION OF PROBLEMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me say at the outset that the government shares the concern of the hon. member for Chapleau (Mr. Laprise) concerning the communities in this country, and more particularly those in northwestern Quebec, which are dependant upon the gold mining industry. To this extent the government is considering the continuation beyond December 31, 1967, of the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act. The Department of Industry of course is concerned with the development of other industries in those areas, and the new manpower centres are operating in such a way as to retrain and redirect labour to new occupations as they develop in the gold mining regions.
The Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act was passed in 1948. As the name indicates, the problems then confronting the gold mining industry were thought to be transitional in nature; this was an emergency measure. It has continued over the intervening years and the amount of assistance has increased. For example, the amount of assistance increased from $580 per miner per annum in the mid-1950's to a figure in the order of $1,400 per miner per annum in 1966. The total extent of federal tax assistance to the gold mining industry this year will be in the order of $15 million. The industry is declining in output. Paced with a fixed price for its products and rising costs, particularly rising wage rates, it has been in a squeeze. It has done a remarkable job in respect of improving productivity. In general the number of mines in this country has dropped roughly in half since 1948. The problem in northwestern Quebec is not unique. It is a problem which is being encountered in Ontario, British Columbia and in other parts of the country. I know there are other mining opportunities in that general area. The other mining industries are able today to pay something in the order of $20 a week more, and they are drawing off mining labour from the gold mines. Pulp and paper and other industries are in that area.
Nevertheless, the government is prepared to continue the emergency gold mining assistance in some form. It is also energetically exploring the possibility of other opportunities for employment in adjoining areas to support these communities in the future.
